subject: Science
title: Reading What a Graph Actually Shows — Step by Step
tipLine: Slower, more deliberate reading of the same kind of graph — no timer.

vocabTerms.definition: the overall direction data moves across the whole graph — not just one point

blocks.heading: Read it in this order
blocks.body: First, read both axis labels and units before looking at the line — that tells you what's actually being measured. Second, look at the overall shape across the whole graph, not just the start or end. A rising line means the value is increasing; a falling line means it's decreasing; a flat line means it has stopped changing, not that it's zero.

blocks.heading: Worked example
blocks.body: A graph shows a runner's heart rate (y-axis, bpm) over a 30-minute run (x-axis, minutes). The line rises for the first 10 minutes, stays flat for 15 minutes, then falls for the last 5. The flat middle section means heart rate held steady — not that the runner stopped. The falling section at the end means heart rate was decreasing, likely as the run ended.

blocks.question: A graph shows a phone's battery percentage (y-axis) over hours of use (x-axis). The line falls steadily for 6 hours, then stays flat for 2 hours. What does the flat part most likely mean?
options: The phone has no battery left
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right — a flat line means that value has stopped changing, not that it's charging or empty.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — a flat line just means the value stopped changing at whatever level it was at. It's not rising (charging) or at zero (dead).
